q: A chain has a CDN at 99.99%, a web server pair at 99.99%, a single application server at 99% and a database pair at 99.99%. The budget covers one improvement: upgrade the CDN to 99.999%, or add a second application server. Which?

items: **Second application server**: that tier → **99.99%**, chain about **99.96%**
**CDN upgrade**: only about **98.98%**
**In series the weakest component dominates**
a.foot: **Assumes** independent failures and enough **capacity in the surviving server**.

q: A teammate says two 99% servers in parallel give 99.99%, so the service now meets four nines. What must be true for that claim to hold?

items: **Independent failures**
**Failover must work and be fast**
**Either server can carry the full load alone**
**Rest of the request path** must also reach four nines, because everything **in series multiplies**
a.foot: **Shared power, storage or a common software bug** break the independence assumption and make 99.99% optimistic.

q: Two replicas share one power supply. Can you apply the independent parallel formula to the whole service?
a: Not without modelling the common dependency. Both replicas can fail together when power fails; put the required power supply in series with the replica group, or remove that shared failure domain.

q: An SLA promises 99.99% availability per year, and planned downtime counts. A database upgrade needs 2 hours offline. Can you do it without breaching the SLA?

items: **99.99% allows** (1 - 0.9999) x 525,600 = **52.56 minutes** of downtime a year → **2 hours** alone exceeds it
**Option 1**: upgrade without downtime (a **rolling upgrade** across redundant nodes)
**Option 2**: agree a **maintenance window** outside the **agreed service time**
a.foot: At **99.9%** (**8.76 hours** a year), the 2-hour upgrade would fit.

q: Leadership wants every system in the company engineered for 99.99% availability. Critique the directive.

items: **Cost**: each extra nine and each redundant component costs more → apply it **by criticality**
**Classify** functions as **critical or non-critical**
**Critical** → redundancy and the higher target; **accept lower targets** elsewhere
a.foot: The architect's job is to meet the **required availability at acceptable cost**, not to maximise it everywhere.

q: After load shedding is enabled at 80% CPU, incoming traffic to a service doubles within a minute. What is happening, and what is the fix?

a.lead: **Retry spikes**: rejected clients retry immediately, adding load to an already overloaded service.
items: **Retry policy**: limits and **backoff** on clients, alongside the **shedding threshold**
**Per-user rate limits** for greedy clients
a.foot: **Shedding without retry control** can make overload worse.

q: Last year's 14 hours of downtime came mostly from the monthly release process. What kind of downtime is this, and what would you change?

items: **Release windows → planned downtime** → reduced by **continuous delivery and deployment**
**Failed releases → unplanned downtime** → reduced by **phased rollouts** and **systematic rollback**
a.foot: Changing the **release process** likely cuts more downtime than adding **hardware redundancy**, which does not fix bad deployments.

q: One API client's nightly batch job floods a shared service and slows everyone else down. Which cloud-level cause is this, and how would you fix it?

items: **Rate limits per user or API key** (or per IP address)
**Sized** so normal clients are unaffected
a.foot: **Cost**: the batch client must spread its load or negotiate a **higher quota**.

q: Behind a load balancer, instance 1 crashes, then instance 2 crashes 20 minutes later, then the rest go within 10 minutes. What is the likely cause, and how would you confirm it?

items: **Same logic on all instances** → a bug such as a **memory leak** triggered by a particular operation kills the **busiest instance first**
**Survivors take its load** → fail faster
**Confirm**: check **memory growth** and the **request mix** on each instance before it crashed
a.foot: **Adding instances only delays the collapse**; fix or isolate the triggering operation.

q: For a marketing campaign the front end scales from 6 to 75 instances (3,000 threads), while the back end stays at 6 instances with 450 threads. What fails first, and what would you change?

items: **Many fan-ins, bounded capacity**: far more concurrent calls than its **450 threads** can serve
→ requests **queue**, **time out** and trigger **retries**
**Fix**: scale the back end **in step**, or cap calls with **backpressure** or **rate limits**
**Load-test** with the scaled-out front end

q: After a full restart, the database hits 100% CPU and the system takes 40 minutes to recover, although normal load is 30% CPU. Diagnose it and suggest a fix.

items: **Cause**: every service warms its **in-memory cache** from the database at the same moment, just as the database is recovering
**Fix**: bring services back **gradually**, not all at once
**Limit the rate of cache-fill queries** so the database is not swamped

q: A user with 30 million followers posts, and the notification service falls an hour behind. Which failure source is this, and what would you consider?

a.lead: **A heavy operation from a special user**: one action fans out to millions of deliveries.
items: **Handle such accounts differently**: e.g. **fetch their posts when followers read** rather than pushing to every follower
**Isolate their processing** so it cannot starve normal users

q: A product page calls a recommendations service that sometimes hangs for 30 s. Design the protection: timeout, circuit-breaker behaviour and fallback.

items: **Timeout**: short, well below the page's response target, with **at most one retry**

sub: **Opens** after repeated failures and **fails fast**
**Half-open**: tests the service with **trial calls**
**Closes** again on success

items: **Fallback**: a generic list such as **best-sellers**
**Log state changes** for operators
a.foot: **Trade-off**: customers see less personalised pages while the breaker is open.

q: Payments and report generation share one database connection pool of 50. A slow report query exhausts the pool, and payments fail. What would you change?

items: **Separate connection pools** (or separate instances) for payments and reports
→ a report **cannot exhaust** the resources payments need
a.foot: **Cost**: less efficient sharing; one pool may sit idle while the other waits.

q: A fault tree for 'checkout unavailable' has minimal cut sets {DNS failure}, {primary database fails AND replica fails} and {payment gateway down}. Where do you focus first?

a.lead: **Focus on the singletons: DNS and the payment gateway.**
items: **Single-element cut sets**: each alone takes checkout down
**DNS** → add redundant DNS
**Payment gateway** → a second gateway, or a **degraded mode** such as holding orders for later payment
**Database** needs **two failures together** → already protected
a.foot: Provided the primary and replica really **fail independently**.

q: A team wants to start chaos engineering by randomly killing production database nodes next week. Critique the plan.

items: **Prerequisites**: **tracing and monitoring** that show the agreed service outcome
**State a hypothesis** ('losing one replica does not raise checkout errors')
**Inject a targeted, contained fault**
**Analyse** the result
**Only then automate and repeat**
a.foot: **Random destruction** without monitoring and a hypothesis teaches nothing and risks **real outages**.

q: A booking service keeps user sessions in local memory and must survive one server failure. Active/passive or active/active?

a.lead: **Active/active, if you can externalise the sessions** → more capacity.
items: **Active/active**: spreads load across live servers; survives one loss **only if sessions move** out of local memory into a **shared store**
**Active/passive**: simpler, but sessions are **lost at failover** unless replicated, and the **standby sits idle**
**Floating IP** (both): moves the **address, not the state**

q: You have four 3 TB disks, must survive any two disk failures, and need at least 6 TB usable. Which RAID level, and why not RAID 10?

items: **RAID 6**: two disks' worth of **parity** → **6 TB usable**, survives **any two failures**
**Not RAID 10**: also 6 TB but guarantees only **one failure**; two failures in the **same mirror** lose data
a.foot: **Cost**: RAID 6 pays with **parity overhead on writes**.

q: Two disks fail in a four-disk RAID 10 array. Is the data necessarily lost?
a: It depends on placement. One failure in each mirror leaves a working copy; both failures in the same mirror lose that stripe's copies. A failure count alone is insufficient.

q: A team says: 'We have a backup server with nightly copies of all files, so we have server redundancy.' Do you agree?

items: **Backup server supports recovery**, not **live compute failover**
**If the main server fails** → service down until a **restore and rebuild** finish
→ **long recovery time**, up to **a day of changes lost**
**Server redundancy** needs a **prepared standby** or **active peers with current state**

q: A full backup runs Sunday night and incrementals run Monday to Friday nights. The disk fails on Saturday afternoon. What must you restore, and how would differential backups compare?

items: **Incrementals**: restore **Sunday's full**, then **all five incrementals** (Monday to Friday) **in order**; losing any one **breaks the chain**
**Differentials**: restore **Sunday's full** and only **Friday's differential** → simpler and faster
a.foot: Either way, **Saturday's changes** since Friday night are lost.

q: A full backup takes 6 hours, the nightly window is 2 hours, and a full restore must finish within 4 hours. Which backup scheme fits?

items: **Nightly full doesn't fit**: 6 hours vs the 2-hour window
**Differential** is smaller than a full; a restore needs only **two sets**
**Check**: late-week differentials still fit the **2-hour window**, and full + differential restores within **4 hours**
a.foot: **Incrementals** fit the window best but make restores **slower and more fragile**.

q: A manager wants to remove the standby database because 'we already take hourly incremental backups'. Do you agree?

items: **Backups are a recovery measure** that affects **MTTR**, not live redundancy
**Restore** from a full plus many incrementals → **hours**, and loses up to **an hour of data**
**Standby** → takes over in **minutes**
a.foot: **Keep both**, or accept the much longer outage **explicitly**.

q: A design has two load-balanced web servers behind one load balancer, with one database and one shared file system. Where are the single points of failure?

items: **The load balancer** → fix with a **hot standby**
**The database**
**The shared file system**
**Any single firewall or network link** on the path
a.foot: **Redundancy at the web tier** does not make the whole service redundant → check **every required dependency**.

q: The requirement is to survive the loss of an entire data centre and recover within 5 minutes. The current design is a high-availability topology at one site. What must change?

a.lead: **Add wide area load balancing** across a **second site**.
items: **Second site** has its own firewalls, load balancers, web servers, database and file system
**Data replicated** between the sites
→ removes the **single-site failure domain**
a.foot: **Cost**: roughly **double the infrastructure** plus the complexity of **cross-site data replication**.

q: An internal HR tool needs 99% availability, and a payments API needs 99.99%. Which availability patterns would you pick for each?

items: **HR tool (99%)**: a **basic or load-balanced web application** is likely enough; 99% allows about **3.65 days** of downtime a year

sub: Redundant **load balancers**, **clusters** and **data tier**
Possibly a **second site**
**End-to-end availability calculated** and **failover tested**

a.foot: Each step up costs more → **match the pattern to the required nines**.

q: A team says Kubernetes will make their single-instance database highly available because it restarts failed pods. Do you agree?

items: **Restarting or rescheduling the pod** → shortens recovery
But the **database is still down** while it restarts
A restart gives the data **no redundant copy**
**Node or storage failure** can still lose service or data
a.foot: Add **replication across nodes**, or a **managed redundant database**, and **test recovery**.

q: A two-node active/passive database cluster uses one shared storage array, and the array fails. What happens, and what alternative avoids it?

items: **Shared disk** delegates redundancy to the storage → the **array is a single point of failure**
**Shared-nothing**: each node owns its storage and data is **replicated** → avoids it
a.foot: **Cost**: managing **replication and promotion**.

q: A primary/replica database loses its primary at peak time. What happens to reads and writes, and what does recovery involve?

items: **Reads** can continue on the **replica**
**Writes stop** until a replica is **promoted** to primary, because only the primary accepts writes
**Promotion takes time**; writes **not yet replicated may be lost**
a.foot: **Read replicas** provide read capacity and redundancy, not **independent write leaders**.

q: Application instances are spread across two availability zones, but the database runs in one zone and is protected by periodic snapshots. That zone fails. What happens?

a.lead: **Compute survives, but the service loses its data tier.**
items: **Restoring from a snapshot** takes time and loses **every change since the snapshot**
**Spreading compute alone is not enough**
**Fix**: **replicate the database across zones**, or plan an explicit **data recovery** that meets the **recovery target**

q: A web system has an active/passive load balancer pair (99% each), two web servers in parallel (99% each), one application server (99%), an active/passive database pair (99% each) and one firewall (98%). The target is 99.9%. Calculate end-to-end availability, say whether it meets the target, and recommend improvements with their assumptions.

a.lead: **96.99%: misses 99.9%**; replicating the app server and firewall gives **99.92%**.
items: **In series**: 0.9999^3 x 0.99 x 0.98 = **96.99%** → misses **99.9%** badly because of the **single application server and firewall**
**Replicate both**: 0.9999^4 x (1 - 0.02^2) = **99.92%** → just meets the target
**Assumes**: **independent failures**, **working failover** and **enough capacity in the survivors**
a.foot: **Shared power, storage or a common software fault** would lower the real figure → **test failover** and check for **shared failure domains**.

q: A monthly SLA promises 99.95% over a 30-day, 24-hour service month. This month had a 15-minute unplanned outage and a 20-minute planned maintenance window. Does the service meet the SLA? What changes the answer, and what would you change in the design?

a.lead: **Passes if planned maintenance is excluded; fails if it counts.**
items: **Month** = **43,200 minutes**; **99.95%** allows **21.6 minutes** of downtime
**Outage alone**: 15 minutes (**99.965%**) → **passes**
**Planned maintenance counts**: total 35 minutes (**99.919%**) → **fails**
**What changes the answer**: whether the **agreed service time excludes the maintenance window**

sub: **Rolling or blue/green deployments** → maintenance needs no downtime
**Faster detection and failover** → shorter unplanned outages

q: Service A receives 100 requests/s and has 200 worker threads. Each request calls service B with a 30 s timeout. B slows from 50 ms to 10 s per call. Explain what happens to A, and design the containment.

sub: **Little's Law**: A needs 100 x 10 = **1,000** requests in flight but has **200 threads**
→ pool **exhausted within about 2 seconds**
→ A stops responding and **its own callers fail**, made worse by **retries**
**Short timeout**: 1 s would keep about **100 requests** in flight
**Circuit breaker**: fails fast with a **fallback** once B is unhealthy
**Bulkhead**: calls to B use their own limited pool, so they cannot take every thread
**Bounded retries with backoff**

items: **Validate**: inject latency into B in a **chaos experiment**

q: An e-commerce site needs 99.99% availability for checkout. The data tier is the weak point. Compare two database redundancy models and recommend one, stating what you would monitor.

a.lead: **Prefer shared-nothing replication across failure domains** for 99.99%.
items: **Active/passive with shared disk**: simple failover, but the **shared storage is a single point of failure** unless the array itself is redundant

**Shared-nothing replication** (a primary with replicas, or multi-node replication): each node has **its own storage** → avoids that, but needs **promotion rules** and risks **losing unreplicated writes** at failover

sub: **Automated, tested promotion** and **enough capacity in the survivors**
Plus **RAID** and **tested backups** for recovery
**Replication lag**
**Failover time** and **data loss** in failover tests

a.foot: **Calculate end-to-end availability** rather than trusting the topology label.

q: A database holds 2 TB. A full backup takes 5 hours, the nightly window is 2 hours, daily changes are about 50 GB, and the recovery-time target is 3 hours. Compare full, differential and incremental backup and recommend a scheme.

a.lead: **Weekly full + nightly differentials**, if day-six differentials fit the window.
items: **Nightly full**: **impossible** (5 hours against a 2-hour window)
**Weekly full + nightly incrementals**: copies only about **50 GB** a night, but a late-week restore needs the full plus **up to six incrementals in order** → **slowest and most fragile**
**Weekly full + nightly differentials**: grows to about **300 GB by day six**, which must still fit the window; restore needs only **the full plus one differential**
**Then test** whether a **2 TB full restore** can finish within **3 hours**
a.foot: If it cannot, **backups alone cannot meet the target** → you need a **standby replica**.

q: Choose a RAID level for an array of four 3 TB disks that must tolerate any two simultaneous disk failures, and state its cost against the alternatives.

items: **Tolerance**: guarantees **any two disk failures**, with at least **four disks**
**Capacity**: two disks' worth holds **parity** → four 3 TB disks provide **6 TB usable**
**Cost**: **parity updates add write overhead**; actual speed depends on workload and implementation

sub: **RAID 10**: same **6 TB** but guarantees only **one failure** (two only if they are in **different mirrors**)
**RAID 5**: **9 TB** with **one-failure** tolerance
**RAID 0**: **no protection**

q: A vendor offers a server with a 30% faster CPU clock. Your application spends 70% of each request waiting on the database. Will throughput rise by 30%?

items: **Throughput reflects the whole system** → here the **database dominates**
A faster CPU speeds up only the small **CPU share** of the work
**Measure throughput** under your own workload before paying for **clock speed**
a.foot: Upgrading the **bottleneck resource** (the database, or how it is used) is what raises throughput.

q: A dashboard shows CPU at 20%, and the team concludes performance is fine. Users report 8-second responses. What is wrong with the conclusion?

a.lead: **Low utilisation is not proof of good performance.**
items: **Time spent waiting on another resource**: database locks, disk, a slow dependency, the network
Or the **CPU may be idle** because work is **stuck elsewhere**
**Look together** at response time, throughput and the **utilisation of each resource** → find where the time goes

q: A load test fires requests back-to-back from 500 virtual users with zero think time. Real users pause about 10 s between actions, and responses take about 1 s. What does the test misrepresent?

items: **No think time**: 500 users generate about **500 requests/s**
**10 s pause**: 500 / (10 + 1) → roughly **45 requests/s**
→ the test therefore models a **far heavier load** than 500 real users
a.foot: Set realistic **think times** and **arrival rates**, or the results won't map to the requirement.

q: Average response time rose from 300 ms to 2 s while service time stayed at 250 ms. Where did the extra time go, and how would you confirm it?

a.lead: **Response time = service time + waiting time + transmission time.**
items: **Service unchanged** → the growth is almost certainly **waiting in queues** caused by **higher utilisation**
Or possibly **transmission**
**Confirm**: check **queue lengths**, **utilisation** and **network timings** at each tier

q: Three tiers in series take 50, 100 and 600 ms per request and have capacities of 40, 12 and 25 requests/s. Which tier do you work on to cut response time, and which to raise throughput?

items: **Response time** → the **600 ms tier**, which is the largest share of the 750 ms total
**Throughput** → the **12 requests/s tier**, which caps the pipeline
a.foot: They are different tiers: the biggest contributor to response time is not necessarily the **capacity bottleneck**, so measure both.

q: Four tiers have throughputs 10, 16, 6 and 20 tps in series. What is system throughput, and what happens if you double the DB?
a: System throughput is min = 6 tps (app server). Doubling the DB changes nothing because the app server remains the bottleneck.

q: A system can complete at most 20 requests/s and receives 22/s for an hour. What happens to throughput and response time?

items: **Excess 2 requests/s** → either **queue** or are **rejected**
**Unbounded queue** → about **7,200 requests** waiting after an hour
**Response time keeps climbing** → no steady state
a.foot: **Add capacity** or **shed or throttle load**; waiting it out does not help.

q: A page calls three services in parallel, taking 120, 300 and 80 ms, and needs all three results. A teammate estimates 500 ms for the page. Do you agree?

a.lead: **No**: the page takes about **300 ms** plus coordination overhead.
items: **Branches that run concurrently contribute their maximum**
**Speed up the 300 ms service**; improving the other two changes nothing
a.foot: If the calls were **sequential**, the teammate's sum would be right.

q: Each request uses 40 ms of application CPU and makes 3 database calls of 20 ms each. At 15 requests/s, which resource saturates first, and at what request rate?

a.lead: **The database saturates first**, at about **16.7 requests/s**.
items: **Service demand**: CPU 40 ms; database 3 x 20 = 60 ms
**At 15 requests/s**: database 15 x 0.06 = **90% busy**; CPU 60%
**Saturation**: database at 1 / 0.06 → about 16.7 requests/s
a.foot: Cutting **database visits per request** (for example by **batching** or **caching**) raises that limit more than a faster CPU would.

q: A gateway forwards 125 packets/s, taking 2 ms each. What is its utilisation, and at what rate does it saturate?
a: U = 125 x 0.002 = 25%. It saturates at 1 / 0.002 = 500 packets/s. Response time will rise sharply well before that point because of queueing, so don't plan to run it near 100%.

q: A colleague says you cannot apply the Utilization Law because the arrivals are bursty, not Poisson. Do you agree?

items: **Operational laws are identities** over measured quantities → **U = XS** holds for the observed interval, whatever the **arrival distribution**
What does need **distribution assumptions** is predicting **queueing delay**, as in **M/M/1**
Keep the **units**, **interval** and **system boundary** consistent

q: A server has a pool of 40 threads. Requests arrive at 100/s and spend 0.3 s each in the server. Is the pool big enough, and what if a slow dependency raises the time to 0.6 s?

items: **At 0.3 s**: by **Little's Law**, n = 100 x 0.3 = **30 requests** in the server → fits within 40 threads

items.t: **At 0.6 s**: n = **60** → more than the pool
sub: Requests **queue for threads** → response time climbs further
The failure can **cascade upstream**

a.foot: **Protects against this**: a **timeout** on the dependency, or a **larger pool**.

q: Measured per-visit response times: CPU 0.25 s over 181 visits, storage A 0.203 s over 80 visits, storage B 0.071 s over 100 visits. Which contributes most to the 68.6 s job time, and what does that suggest?

items: **Storage A**: 0.203 x 80 → about **16.2 s**
**Storage B**: 0.071 x 100 → about **7.1 s**
→ the **CPU dominates**, mostly because of its **visit count**
a.foot: Reduce the CPU's **visits** or its **per-visit time** before tuning storage.

q: A shop serves 15 customers an hour, and you observe an average of 3 customers inside. How long does a customer spend in the shop?
a: R = n / λ = 3 / 0.25 per minute = 12 minutes. That includes both waiting and service, because n counted everyone inside. Use the same boundary for n and R.

q: Orders arrive at 20 an hour, and one server completes 30 an hour, giving a 6-minute average time in system. The target is under 3 minutes. Would a server that completes 45 an hour meet it?

items: **Utilisation** falls from 67% to 44% → that is where the **waiting time** goes
a.foot: This assumes random (**Poisson**) arrivals and **exponential service**, so validate with measured data.

q: Average utilization is 75%, so why is there still a queue?
a: Arrivals are random and bursty. A burst of jobs arrives faster than the server can handle even though the average load is below capacity, so waiting occurs; response time rises as 1/(1 - U).

q: To save money, a team plans to run its application servers at 90% CPU. Service time is 1 s, and the response target is 3 s. Under M/M/1, is the plan safe?

items: **M/M/1**: R = S / (1 - U) gives **10 s at 90%**, far over target
**Meeting 3 s** needs **U of 2/3 or less**: 1 / (1 - 0.67) = 3
a.foot: Size the **headroom** from the response target and measured workload; there is **no universally safe percentage**.

q: Arrivals and service capacity are both 30 requests/hour. Can M/M/1 predict a finite mean response time?
a: No. U = 1, so the steady-state denominator µ - λ is zero. The model requires λ < µ; equality leaves no spare capacity to drain random bursts.

q: A bank branch has 4 tellers. Should each teller have their own line, or should one shared line feed all four?

items: **Identical tellers** → a free teller always takes the next customer
**Separate lines** can leave one teller idle while another line waits
a.foot: This assumes every teller can serve every customer; **specialised counters** change the comparison.

q: You need to triple capacity: one server three times faster, or three servers? Give the performance answer and the availability answer.

items: **Response time**: the lecture's ideal model favours **one fast server**, then **three servers sharing a queue**, then **three separate queues**
**Availability**: the single fast server is a **single point of failure**, while three servers survive one loss
a.foot: Most production systems accept slightly higher response time for that **redundancy**.

q: A sizing target says 'queueing below 3 minutes', and service takes 1.5 minutes. What response-time limit should you test?
a: R = waiting + service, so require R < 4.5 minutes. Comparing a response-time formula directly with 3 minutes would impose a different, stricter target.

q: Server A costs $10,000 and delivers 500 tps. Server B costs $3,000 and delivers 120 tps. Which has better price/performance, and what else would you check?

items: **A**: $20 per tps
**B**: $25 per tps

sub: **Operating costs** and **expected lifetime** (Google counted both when choosing **commodity servers**)
The impact of **losing one large server** versus one small one
Whether the load comes in **steps** that suit smaller units

q: Adding a second server behind a load balancer halved average response time, although each request's processing time did not change. Why?

items: **Each server's utilisation roughly halved** → requests spend far less time **waiting in queues**
**Response time = waiting + service**; the **service time is unchanged**
a.foot: To cut service time, you would need **faster processing** or **parallel work** within the request itself.

q: A load balancer uses least-connections with sticky sessions. After a campaign, one server holds 60% of active users and is overloaded. Diagnose it and fix it.

items: **Diagnosis**: **stickiness overrides the balancing policy** → users stay pinned to the server that first held their **session**
**Fix**: move **session state** out of the servers into a **shared store** → any server can take any request
a.foot: The cost is a **network hop** to the state store.

q: A partner's month-end batch job floods the system with requests, and interactive users time out. Which tactic family applies, and what would you do?

items: **Manage the arrival rate** → throttle the partner
**Prioritise input** → interactive requests go ahead of batch
a.foot: The batch job takes longer as a result. **Adding resources** would also work, but costs more for a **predictable monthly peak**.

q: Servers of different sizes (8 and 32 cores) sit behind a round-robin load balancer, and the small ones are overloaded. What would you change?

items: **Round robin ignores capability** → the 8-core servers get the same share as the 32-core ones
**Fix**: use a **capability-weighted** or **server-load** policy, or **least response time** → work follows actual capacity

q: Cache access takes 8 ms, the source takes 50 ms, and the hit ratio is 20%. Is the cache worth it? If cache access were 15 ms, what hit ratio would you need?

items: **At 8 ms**: 0.2 x 8 + 0.8 x (8 + 50) = **48 ms** against 50 ms without the cache → a **small gain**
**At 15 ms**: expected time = 15 + (1 - h) x 50, which must be under 50
→ **h must exceed 30%**
a.foot: Below that, the cache adds **cost and latency**.

q: A social app's feed reads outnumber posts 50 to 1, and one account has 20 million followers. Fan-out on write, fan-out on read, or a hybrid?

items: **Fan-out on write** precomputes timelines → the dominant **reads are cheap**
**20-million-follower account**: writing to every follower's timeline on each post is **too costly** → **merge its posts in at read time**
a.foot: Trade-off: extra **read-time work** for followers of such accounts, as in the lecture's **Twitter** example.

q: With 15 GB of cache and data types A (10 GB, 10 ms), B (20 GB, 30 ms), C (30 GB, 10 ms), what do you cache?

items: **Full-cache average benefit/GB** ranks **B, A, C**
But **B needs 20 GB** for its measured 30 ms gain, and there is only **15 GB**
→ measure **partial hit ratios** and **marginal benefits**, then allocate the available space
a.foot: The full-cache ratios alone do not prove the best split.

q: A product catalogue has 1 million items. In shop X, access is spread evenly across them; in shop Y, it follows a power law. A cache holds 1% of the items. Where does it help?

items: **Shop Y, power law**: a small set of **popular items** gets most of the requests → 1% of items can yield a **high hit ratio**
**Shop X, uniform access**: a 1% cache gives roughly a **1% hit ratio** → not worth it
a.foot: Measure the **access distribution** before sizing a cache.

q: A matching job takes 2 s for 10,000 candidates using an O(n^2) algorithm. Data will grow to 100,000. Would you buy 10x hardware or change the algorithm?

items: **O(n^2)** means **100 times** the work → about **200 s**
Even with **10x hardware** that scales perfectly → still takes about **20 s**, and every further growth repeats the problem
**O(n log n)** → grows only about **12.5 times** for 10 times the data
a.foot: Verify with **measurements at the expected size**, because **constants and I/O** also matter.

q: Scoring every candidate-job pair currently happens in the application server, which pulls all the rows over the network to return the top 1,000. When should the scoring move into the database server?

a.lead: **When the data volume is large and the result small**, as here.
items: **Running it in the database** → transfers only **1,000 results** instead of every row
**Trade-off**: load on the **database server**, which is usually **harder to scale** → check its **spare capacity** first

q: A 'friends of friends within 3 hops' query on a relational store takes 9 seconds. What would you investigate?

items: **The data store**, which is often the bottleneck
First the **indexes** on the relationship tables
Then whether the **storage technology fits** → relationship-heavy traversals like this suit a **graph database**
a.foot: Switching stores is costly → **prove the gain with a prototype** first.

q: One API customer sends 25 large requests at once, and everyone else's requests wait behind them. What would you add?

items: **Per-client rate limits**
Plus **fair queueing** or **separate lanes**
→ one demanding client or burst cannot **starve** the others
a.foot: That customer's batch then takes longer, which you can offer as a **paid higher limit** if it matters.

q: A team will adopt a message broker none of them has used, with a target of 2,000 messages/s at peak. What would you do before the full build?

items: **Set the goal**: 2,000 messages/s at the required latency
**Decide how much to build**
**Instrument** it
**Run it at the target load**
**Repeat** until the risk is contained
a.foot: **Unknown technology** is exactly where you should **fail early**. Trade-off: confidence against prototyping effort.

q: Two developers time the search API from home with a browser tool and get 0.8 s and 4 s. Why are the results unreliable, and how would you test properly?

sub: The **client, network and load are uncontrolled**
Each person sends a **handful of requests** → the numbers reflect their connections, not the system under its **required load**

items.t: **Proper test**: a **scripted load test** from a **controlled environment**
sub: Defined **arrival rate**, **think time** and **request mix**
Report **percentiles** against the target

a.foot: A **queueing model** or **simulation** can complement it.

q: A performance document shows only one box diagram: front end, service layer, back ends. What is missing?

items: **Sequence diagram**: call order and **loops**, such as **repeated back-end calls** per request
**Data flow**: **large messages**, calls that carry **many records**, and **high-frequency interactions**
a.foot: Aim for the level of detail where these become visible, without drawing every class.

q: A request passes a firewall (5 ms wait, 45 ms service, 10 tps capacity), a reverse proxy (10, 90, 16 tps), an app server (50, 550, 6 tps) and a database (30, 300, 20 tps), with 200 ms of network latency. (a) Find the response time and throughput. (b) You add a second app server. What is the new throughput, and what is the next bottleneck?

sub: Response time = 50 + 100 + 600 + 330 = 1080 ms
Plus 200 ms latency → **1280 ms**
Throughput = min(10, 16, 6, 20) = **6 tps**, limited by the **app server**
Two app servers give about 12 tps
Throughput = min(10, 16, 12, 20) = **10 tps** → the **firewall** is now the **bottleneck**
Each request's **service time is unchanged** → response time improves only through **less queueing** at the app tier

a.foot: To go beyond 10 tps, **scale the firewall** as well.

q: Each job needs 5 s of CPU, 80 I/Os on storage A (50 ms each) and 100 I/Os on storage B (30 ms each). Storage A is observed at 15.70 I/Os per second. Find the system throughput, the utilisations and the bottleneck. What would it take to double throughput?

items: **Demands**: CPU 5 s, A 4 s, B 3 s
**Bottleneck**: the **CPU**; maximum throughput = 1 / 5 = **0.2 jobs/s**

items.t: **To double** to about 0.39 jobs/s: every demand must fall below about **2.56 s**
sub: Halving CPU demand alone leaves **A** as the limit at 1 / 4 = 0.25 jobs/s
So **storage A**, and **storage B** (3 s), also need **faster devices**, **fewer visits** or **more parallel units**

a.foot: **Bottlenecks move** as you fix them.

q: A shop receives 20 requests an hour, and one server handles 30 an hour. Compute the utilisation and average time in system. Then, at 2 requests per minute with a 1.5-minute service time and a target of queueing under 3 minutes, a faster server is not possible: how many servers do you need with separate queues, and with one shared queue?

sub: **R = 6 minutes** including service
**Offered load** is 3 → **ρ = 3/c**
Waiting under 3 minutes → **R < 4.5**
**Separate queues** need **c = 5**
The lecture's approximate **shared-queue** model gives **c = 4**
Both need **ρ < 1**

a.foot: Validate the chosen model with **measured data** and add **headroom for a server failure**.

q: 1000 players each trigger an event every 3 s (think time). Server time is 50 ms and the round trip is 200 ms. What load must the server handle, and how many requests are in flight?

a.lead: Assuming **one outstanding request per player** and **no queueing**:
items: **Work in the server** averages 307.7 x 0.05 = **15.4 requests**
**In flight**, including network time: 307.7 x 0.25 = **76.9 requests**
a.foot: State the **boundary** you are counting; the remaining players are **thinking**.

q: A product-detail lookup takes 50 ms from the database. A cache would take 5 ms. Measured access is uniform across the catalogue, and a cache the size you can afford gives a 20% hit ratio. A teammate says to add the cache. Argue for or against, and say what would change your mind.

items: **Expected time** = 0.2 x 5 + 0.8 x 55 = **45 ms** against 50 ms → a **10% gain**
**Cost**: the **cache memory** and an **extra component**
**Stops paying** at all if cache access reaches 10 ms or the hit ratio falls
**Uniform access** → a larger cache raises hits only **in proportion to its size**

sub: A **power-law access pattern**, where a small cache catches most requests
**Precomputing** the expensive part of the page
A source that is **much slower than 50 ms**

a.foot: **Measure before buying.**

q: A web tier runs at 85% utilisation with 4 s average response time against a 2 s target, and 40% of requests fetch the same home-page data. Which tactics would you apply, in what order, and how would you verify them before building?

items: **First reduce demand**: **cache or precompute** the home-page data → removes up to **40%** of the work, lowering utilisation and queueing

sub: Add servers behind a **load balancer** (**shared queue**) → per-server utilisation falls well below 85%
Fix any **algorithmic** or **database bottleneck** the measurements show

items: **If needed**, **throttle or deprioritise** non-interactive load

sub: A **queueing model** or **simulation** (for example **JMT**)
An **instrumented prototype benchmark** under the **real request mix**
Repeat until the **2 s target** holds with **headroom**

q: A photo app expects 50,000 uploads a day at an average of 3 MB, and keeps 3 copies of each photo. Apply the capacity-planning model to estimate storage growth.

items: **Forecast workload**: 50,000 uploads a day
**Workload-to-resource relationship**: 3 MB x 3 copies = **9 MB per upload**
**Derived capacity**: about **450 GB a day** (decimal units), or roughly **164 TB a year**
**Plus** indexes, logs, overhead and headroom
a.foot: Each input is an **assumption to monitor**: if the upload rate or photo size grows, the estimate scales with it.

q: CPU graphs have risen steadily for months. The business asks what happens if sign-ups double. Can you answer from the system metrics alone?

items: You need **application-level metrics**: sign-ups, uploads, API calls per key
**How each relates to resource use** → turn a **business forecast** into a **resource forecast**
**Start collecting** them alongside the system metrics, and **fit the relationship from history**

q: A new system has no production data yet, and the vendor publishes a benchmark for similar hardware. Which data source would you use, and what is the risk?

a.lead: **Use the vendor benchmark as a starting point.**
items: **Self-benchmark** the significant scenarios if you can
**Risk**: the vendor's **workload and configuration** differ from yours → its numbers may not transfer
Once the system runs → switch to **monitoring data**, which is the **best source**

q: An application writes 20 GB of logs a day and must keep them for 90 days. The busiest day so far produced 35 GB. How much log storage do you plan for?

a.lead: **Disk is cumulative**: plan for everything retained over 90 days, not the peak day.
items: **At the average**: 20 x 90 = **1.8 TB**
**Some days reach 35 GB** → add **headroom** or forecast **growth in the daily rate**
**Plus overhead** for indexes and any replicas

q: Transactions start at 1M a month and grow 10% a month, with 24-month retention and 1 MB per record. A teammate estimates 24 x 1M x 1 MB = 24 TB. Do you agree?

items: Monthly volume is a **geometric series**: 1M x (1.1^24 - 1) / 0.1
→ about **88.5M transactions**, or about **88.5 TB**
→ the teammate's figure is **less than a third** of the need
**Add** fixed overhead, indexes and replicas
a.foot: **Revisit the forecast** as actual growth is observed.

q: After two years, does 24-month retention mean a growing system's storage stops growing?
a: Not necessarily. Old records expire, but newer months may contain more records than the months removed. Forecast the sum within the moving 24-month window using the expected arrival growth.

q: Your 88.5 TB data estimate covers records only. The database adds indexes of about 30% of data size and keeps one full replica. What is the real storage need?

items: **Indexes**: 88.5 x 1.3 → about **115 TB**
**Replica**: doubled → about **230 TB**
**Plus** the fixed OS and database baseline and a buffer
a.foot: **Size data feeds and overheads separately** and state the assumptions, so each can be revised.

q: Storage use rises steadily month by month. A different metric, order volume, spikes every December. Which forecasting approach suits each?

items: **Storage is trending** → fit a **regression** (linear or exponential) and extrapolate
**Orders are seasonal** → model the **yearly cycle** explicitly, for example by comparing each December with previous ones
a.foot: A simple **moving average** or **exponential smoothing** would smooth out the December spike rather than predict it.

q: After a merger, traffic stepped up permanently by 40%. Your exponential-smoothing forecast with alpha = 0.1 still lags far behind. Why, and what would you change?

items: **Why**: a **low alpha** gives little weight to the latest observation → the forecast adjusts slowly to a real **level change**
**Fix**: **raise alpha** so it reacts faster, or **refit** from the post-merger data
a.foot: A **high alpha** also chases noise, so choose it for how quickly real change happens.

q: A linear fit says the disk fills on day 70 and an exponential fit says day 55. Today is day 20, and procurement takes 7 weeks. When do you order?

items: **Lead time**: seven weeks is **49 days**
**Linear forecast** leaves **50 days** → almost no margin
**Exponential forecast** leaves **35** → already **too late**
a.foot: Both are **extrapolations with error**, so plan on the **earlier date plus a buffer**, and keep comparing the fits with new readings.

q: A service averages 200 requests/s, peaks at 900 requests/s on Monday mornings, and its data grows by 5 GB a day. How do you size the servers and the disk?

items: **Servers are peak-driven**: size for **900 requests/s** at the response target, plus **headroom for a node failure**; average load is irrelevant to that
**Disk is cumulative**: size for **5 GB a day** over the **retention period**, plus overhead
a.foot: Using the average for servers, or the peak for disk, would get both wrong.

q: The benchmark shows 17.04 tps on 1 machine, 30.81 on 2 and 55.76 on 4. A teammate plans 8 machines for 136 tps. Do you agree?

items: **Each doubling** has given about **1.8x**, not 2x
→ 8 machines might give about **101 tps** if the trend holds, and it may get worse
The **application servers' CPU** was already at **95-98%** at maximum load
a.foot: **Benchmark 8 machines**, or fit a **scalability model**, before committing.

q: A reporting scenario is 4 times slower than the reference benchmark of 55.76 tps on 4 machines, and the business needs 30 report requests/s. Is 4 machines enough?

items: **Estimated throughput**: 55.76 / 4 → about **13.9 tps**, less than half the need
Adding machines will **not scale linearly**
a.foot: **Reduce the scenario's cost** (precompute, cache, optimise queries) as well as adding capacity, and **benchmark the actual report**.

q: At maximum TPS, the application servers' CPU sits at 97% and the database server's at 2%. A teammate proposes a bigger database server. Respond.

items: The **application tier is the bottleneck**; the database is almost idle
A bigger database adds nothing until the application tier is **scaled out** or made **cheaper per request**
a.foot: **Re-measure** afterwards, because the bottleneck may then **move to the database**.

q: A workload is 90% parallel. Going from 10 to 20 servers, how much speedup do you gain, and what is the ceiling?

items: → doubling the servers gives only about **31% more speedup**
**Ceiling** = 1 / (1 - 0.9) = **10**, however many you add
a.foot: **Reducing the serial part** pays more than adding servers.

q: Throughput rises up to 8 nodes, then falls at 12. Which model explains this, and what does it say about the cause?

a.lead: **USL, not Amdahl**: Amdahl's speedup flattens but never falls.
items: **Cause of the decline**: the **crosstalk (coherency) term, kappa** → nodes spend more and more effort **coordinating** with each other
**Fit sigma and kappa** to the measurements → find the **peak**
**Reduce cross-node coordination** if you need to scale further

q: The parallel fraction P was measured with a load test that sent only login requests. Should you trust the resulting scaling prediction?

items: **P depends on the workload mix**: logins may parallelise well, while **checkouts update shared data serially**
**Unrepresentative test** → the wrong P → the wrong server count
a.foot: Repeat the test with a **production-like mix**.

q: Load tests show that a single shared stock-count row is updated on every order. How does that affect scaling, and what would you change?

items: **Effect**: every order **serialises** on that row → lowers the **parallel fraction P** → caps speedup at **1 / (1 - P)**
**Change**: **reduce the serial part**, for example by **partitioning** the stock count or updating it **asynchronously**
a.foot: Accept the trade-off in **exactness or consistency** of the count.

q: With the lecture's mix, 4 machines give an estimated 38.8 tps. The forecast peak is 50 tps. How many machines would you plan for?

items: **Linear estimate**: 50 / 38.8 → about **1.29 times** the capacity → about **5.2 machines**
**Scaling has been sub-linear** (about 1.8x per doubling) → plan to **benchmark 6 or more** with the production mix
Then add **headroom for a node failure**
a.foot: The **weighted estimate** is a simplified starting point, not deployable capacity.

q: If Payment's share rose from 5% to 10% (taking 5% from Login), what happens to overall throughput?

items: Within the lecture's **weighted estimate**, replacing 5% Login with Payment changes the total by 0.05 x (13.94 - 55.76) = **-2.091 tps**
→ about **36.7 tps**
a.foot: The actual production effect requires **mixed-load measurement**.

q: You have neither a reference benchmark nor a production system. How do you get sizing data?

a.lead: **Run simulated load tests** (for example with **JMeter** or **Artillery**).
items: **Define** the scenarios, the mix and the arrival rates
**Measure** response time and throughput as load increases
a.foot: Once a production system exists, switch to its **monitoring data**, which is the best source.

q: A team sized its servers from a one-hour sample taken on a Tuesday afternoon. What is the risk?

items: **Risk**: the sample hides **daily and weekly cycles**
If the real peak is **Monday morning**, as in the **Flickr** example → servers **undersized** exactly when demand is highest
a.foot: **Measure over weeks**, identify the **recurring peak**, and size for it.

q: A service used only in Asia expands to Europe. How might the load pattern change?

items: **Time zones shift and blend the peaks**: the European peak arrives hours after the Asian one
→ the service is busy for **more hours each day**, and the peaks **may overlap**
a.foot: **Re-measure** after the launch, and size for the **combined peak**, not either region alone.

q: Monday peak busy processes follow the trend y = 42.75x + 726, where x is weeks. Your servers handle 1,600 busy processes in total, and procurement takes 7 weeks. When do you run out, and when must you order?

items: → capacity **runs out around week 20**
With a **7-week lead time plus a buffer** → **order by about week 12 or 13**
a.foot: Check the trend against **new weekly peaks**, since a **steeper trend** moves the date earlier.

q: New instances take 5 minutes to start, and traffic doubles within 3 minutes at 9 am every weekday. How should the scaling work?

a.lead: Use **scheduled scaling** from the historical pattern.
items: **Reactive scaling will always be late** → demand doubles before new instances are ready
**Add capacity shortly before 9 am**
**Scale up aggressively** for unexpected surges
**Scale down conservatively** afterwards → briefly holding spare capacity costs little compared with failing users

q: Two nodes handle 120 requests/s. Scale-out triggers above 55/node and scale-in below 45/node. Why might adding one node cause ping-pong?

items: **Before scale-out**: each handles 60/s
**After adding a third**: each handles 40/s → below the 45/s **scale-in threshold**
**Removing one** returns to 60/s
a.foot: Set **thresholds and adjustments** so the new state does not immediately trigger the opposite action; use **cooldown** as well.

q: The forecast says capacity runs out in 6 weeks. The procurement template totals about 7 weeks, plus 1 week to get downtime approved. What do you do now, and what do you change for next time?

a.lead: **You are already late** for the normal process.

sub: Look for **interim capacity**: temporary cloud capacity, expedited delivery, or reducing or throttling demand
**Start procurement immediately**, running the **downtime approval in parallel**

items: **Next time**: trigger procurement from the **forecast** with the **full lead time plus a buffer**
a.foot: Buying very early has its own cost, **tying up money** and **missing price drops**, so plan the date rather than **stockpiling**.

q: A database disk has 280 GB used of 500 GB, and the last 20 days of readings fit a linear trend of about 4.35 GB a day. Procurement takes about 7 weeks, plus 1 week for downtime approval. When does the disk fill, and when must you act? What could make the forecast wrong?

items: **Time to fill**: (500 - 280) / 4.35 → about **51 days**, roughly **7 weeks**
→ the disk fills at about the point a normal **7-week procurement** would deliver
With a **buffer**, and possibly the extra week for **downtime approval** → you must **act now**

sub: Growth may be **exponential rather than linear** → brings the date forward
**Logs and indexes** may grow faster than the data
**20 days of history is short**

a.foot: **Compare linear and exponential fits**, keep revising with new readings, and **plan from the earlier date**.

q: Estimate storage for 1 million transactions a month growing 10% a month, retained for 2 years, at 1 MB per record, with indexes adding 30% and one replica. Then explain what happens to storage in year 3.

items: **First 24 months**: 1M x (1.1^24 - 1) / 0.1 → about **88.5M records**, or **88.5 TB**
With **30% for indexes** → about **115 TB**
With the **replica** → about **230 TB**
**Plus** the fixed OS and database baseline and a buffer

sub: The oldest months **expire**
But each new month (about **9.8M records** by month 25) is far larger than the month it replaces (**1M**)

a.foot: Forecast the **moving 24-month window**, not a one-off total.

q: The 4-machine reference benchmark gives 55.76 tps. Slowness factors are Login 1.0, Search 2.0, Details 1.5, Cart 1.5, Checkout 2.0 and Payment 4.0, and the mix is 30/20/15/20/10/5%. The forecast peak is 45 tps, and the business wants to survive one machine failure. Estimate the capacity and recommend a machine count.

items: **Weighted estimate**: 16.73 + 5.58 + 5.58 + 7.43 + 2.79 + 0.70 → about **38.8 tps** on 4 machines, short of 45 tps
**Sub-linear scaling** (about 1.8x per doubling) → 45 tps needs more than a proportional **4.6 machines**
**Survive one failure** → the survivors must still deliver 45 tps
If the 1.8x-per-doubling trend holds, **5 machines** give about **47 tps**
→ **plan for 6** (5 survivors after a failure), and confirm it by **benchmarking with the production mix**
a.foot: The estimate assumes **uniform slowness across tiers** and the **benchmark's configuration**, so validate it with a **mixed load test**.

q: Load tests measure 1,000 req/s on 1 node, 1,800 on 2, 3,000 on 4 and 3,200 on 8. Explain the pattern, estimate what 16 nodes would give, and recommend what to do.

items: **Pattern**: returns diminish quickly; 4 to 8 nodes adds only **7%**
**Suggests** a large **serial part** (shared data, quotas) and possibly **crosstalk**

items.t: **16 nodes** may give little or even **less than 3,200 req/s**
sub: **Amdahl** caps speedup at 1 / (1 - P)
**USL** allows throughput to **fall past a peak**
**Fit USL's sigma and kappa** to these points → find the peak
**Don't buy 16 nodes** without testing
Better value comes from **reducing the serial work**, such as **shared-row updates** or **cross-node coordination**
**Rerun the tests** with a production-like mix

q: Design an auto-scaling policy for a web tier with a Monday 9 am peak of 900 requests/s, nodes that handle 100 requests/s at the response target, and a 3-minute start-up time. Include thresholds that avoid ping-pong.

items: **Scheduled scaling** from the weekly trend → about **10 nodes** before 9 am: 9 for the load, plus 1 for headroom
**React to surprises**: scale up **aggressively**, since start-up takes 3 minutes; scale down **conservatively** with a **cooldown**
**Thresholds**, for example: scale out above **80 requests/s per node**, scale in below **50**

sub: 4 nodes at 80 = 320 requests/s, spread over 5 nodes, gives **64** → above the scale-in threshold
5 nodes at 50 = 250, over 4 nodes, gives **62.5** → below the scale-out threshold
So **neither action immediately triggers the other**

a.foot: **Revisit the thresholds** as the Monday trend grows.

q: Two designs for a loyalty system: A ships in 2 months with the reward rules hard-coded; B takes 3 months with the rules isolated behind an interface and held in configuration. Marketing expects to change the rules monthly for 5 years. Which do you choose?

items: **About 60 rule changes** expected → the extra month is repaid by **cheaper, safer changes**
**Most lifecycle cost falls in maintenance** (the lecture cites **80-90%**)
**A** would need a **code change, test and release** for every rule tweak
a.foot: If the system were a **short-lived campaign**, A would be the better choice.

q: A team says it will 'make the code maintainable later, once we have users'. Do you agree?

items: **Detailed refactoring can wait**
**Boundaries, interfaces and variation points** are **architectural** → cost far more to add once code depends on their absence
Put them **where change is likely** now, and defer the rest
a.foot: How much to invest depends on the **expected changes** and the **system's lifetime**.

q: For an insurance product, actuaries change pricing factors monthly, and the screen layout changes about once a year. Which way of incorporating change suits each?

items: **Pricing factors** → **configuration**, or **end-user customisation** by the actuaries: the change is **frequent** and each code change would be expensive
**Layout** → a **code change** is fine: it is **rare**, and the development cost of making it customisable would not pay back
a.foot: Invest in **cheap change where change is likely**.

q: A requirements document says 'the system shall support other payment methods in future' and 'reporting: to be decided in phase 2'. What does this tell the architect?

a.lead: **Open-ended and deferred requirements** signal a **high likelihood of change** → put **variation points** there:
items: A **payment-method interface**
**Reporting** fed from **well-defined data**
a.foot: Spending the same effort on areas with **stable requirements** would be wasted.

q: A B2B SaaS product has five enterprise clients, each with a dedicated implementation team, and each wants its own approval rules. Which change mechanism fits?

items: Build **configurable rules or workflows** that each client's team sets up
**Development cost is high**, but each change is **medium-cost** and needs **no core code change**
**Full end-user customisation** would cost even more to build → isn't needed when **trained implementers** do the changes

q: A team wants to add a fraud-analytics consumer to the existing OrderPlaced events, but the event does not carry the customer's IP address, which the model needs. Is this still a change-free extension?

items: A **new consumer** avoids **producer changes** only when the **existing payload** already meets its needs
Here the **producer must add the field**, ideally as an **optional addition** registered as a **compatible new schema version** → existing consumers keep working
a.foot: Events still **couple consumers** to the payload's **content and meaning**.

q: Five microservices read and write one shared customer table, and renaming a column needs a coordinated release of all five. What has gone wrong?

a.lead: **Shared data has coupled the services**, defeating **independent deployment**.
items: **Fix**: give the customer data a **single owning service**, and have the others use its **API or events**
**Alternative**: if that split is not worth it, a **modular monolith** may contain changes just as well at **lower operational cost**

q: A producer renames the field 'amount' to 'total' and registers the change as version 2 in the schema registry. Are consumers safe?

items: The **registry** stores **versioned schemas** and lets consumers find the one a message uses
But an **incompatible change** still breaks consumers that expect 'amount'

sub: Add 'total' **alongside** 'amount'
**Migrate** the consumers
Only then **remove** the old field

q: In a layered monolith, adding a 'gift card' feature touches the presentation, business and persistence layers. Would a modular monolith help?

items: A **modular monolith** groups code by **business module**
→ a **gift-card module** contains its own UI, logic and data access, and the change stays inside it
a.foot: It still **deploys as one unit**, so you don't get **independent deployment**; that would need **services**.

q: A public API method has 7 parameters, and clients keep breaking whenever a parameter is added. What would you change?

items: **Pass a single request object** → new **optional fields** can be added without changing the **method signature**

items.t: **Old clients must still be served correctly**
sub: Keep existing **fields and meanings**
Give new fields **defaults**
**Test existing consumers**

items: **Version the API** for changes that cannot be compatible

q: A bank receives statements from 12 partners in CSV, XML and fixed-width formats, and parsing logic is spread across the system. What would you change?

items: **Convert at the edge**: each physical format → one **standard logical structure**
Use **only that structure** in the rest of the system
→ a **new partner format** then changes only a **converter**
a.foot: The cost is one more **mapping layer** to maintain.

q: A discount rate of 0.15 is hard-coded in 9 places, and the last change missed one. Which tactic would have prevented this?

items: **Define the rate once**, in configuration or a constant used everywhere → a change never has to be **synchronised across copies**
**Parameterising it in configuration** also lets you change it **without a code release**

q: A JSON API adds a mandatory field to every request. Is it backward compatible because the method signature is unchanged?
a: No. Existing callers omit the new field and may fail validation. Add it as optional with suitable behaviour for old callers, or version the breaking contract and migrate consumers.

q: Each of 30 corporate clients wants a different expense-approval chain, and the chains change a few times a year. How would you design it?

items: An **implementer designs** each client's workflow
It is **stored per tenant**
**At run time** the engine loads and executes it, calling **shared domain logic**
→ changes need **no recompiling or redeployment**
a.foot: The cost is **building or adopting the engine**, and limiting workflows to the steps it supports.

q: For a 3-month MVP, a team proposes fully end-user-customisable reports. Do you agree?

items: **End-user customisation** has the **lowest change cost** when done well, but the **highest development cost**
It needs **strong UX** and **domain understanding** that an MVP rarely has
**Instead**: ship a few **fixed reports** → learn which variations users actually want → add customisation where that demand is clear

q: A checkout error appears in the logs of four services, but nothing links the entries. What would you add?

items: **Created at the entry point** and passed with **every call and event**
**Written in each service's log entries**
→ the entries for one request can be pulled together for **root-cause analysis**
a.foot: **Central log storage alone** does not show which records belong together.

q: Container logs disappear when pods restart, and engineers SSH into nodes to grep for errors. What would you change?

a.lead: **Add the three logging components** (**EFK** is the lecture's example stack):
items: An **agent** on each node that ships logs
**Central log storage**
A **dashboard with search**
→ logs **survive restarts** and can be **searched across services**
a.foot: The cost is running and **sizing the logging infrastructure** itself.

q: A legacy application crashes every night and leaves nothing useful behind. Which analyzability tactics apply?

items: **Automated error detection and reporting**: **core dumps**, **log file monitoring** that raises **alerts**
**Logging** with enough **context** to investigate
**Monitoring through standard protocols** such as **JMX** or **SNMP**
a.foot: Together these turn 'it crashed' into a **diagnosable fault**.

q: The architecture rule says the web layer must not call the persistence layer directly. Code reviews keep missing violations. What would you add?

items: An **automated test** using a **dependency-analysis tool** → **fails the build** when web code depends on persistence packages
It checks the rule on **every build**, which **review cannot do reliably**
a.foot: It guards **only the rules you actually encode**, so add checks for other key characteristics as well.

q: A release breaks checkout, and reverting takes 3 hours because the database migrations cannot be undone. What should the release process have included?

items: **Reversible or backward-compatible migrations**
The ability to **redeploy the previous version quickly**
**Why**: even tested changes fail in production → **fast reversal limits the damage**
a.foot: **Version control**, **automated tests** and **environment configuration as code** make that reversal reliable.

q: A release works in staging but fails in production, because the two environments were configured by hand and differ. A developer suggests committing the production passwords into the repository so everything is in one place. Respond.

items: **Manage environment configuration as code** → staging and production are built from the **same versioned definitions**
**Do not commit secret values** → integrate a **secrets-management tool**, and **reference secrets** from the configuration
a.foot: **Reproducible environments** without **leaked credentials** make change reliable.

q: A quality dashboard improves after a release. Does that prove the architecture is easier to maintain?

items: **Check what changed** in the metrics, and whether they reflect **relevant change** or **diagnostic effort**
**Combine trends** with actual **change scenarios** and **fitness checks**
a.foot: A score is evidence for its **measured properties**, not all maintainability.

q: A manager wants to rank three teams' systems by their static-analysis scores to decide bonuses. Do you agree?

items: These metrics are useful for **tracking one code base's relative progress over time**, not for **comparing different systems** in absolute terms
**Size, language and domain differ** between systems
Using them for **bonuses** also **invites gaming**
a.foot: Compare each team against its **own trend**, alongside **real change effort**.

q: A product's discount and eligibility rules change every quarter, and three of its 20 enterprise clients need their own approval flow. The business wants changes shipped without redeployment. Recommend a design and its costs.

a.lead: **Defer binding** for the kinds of change that recur.
items: **Rule parameters in configuration**, which business users edit through an **admin screen**, behind a **single point of definition**
A **workflow engine** runs **per-tenant approval flows** designed by the **implementation team**
**Encapsulate the domain actions** the workflows call, and define the **supported variation points**
**Costs**: this lowers the cost of each change but **raises development cost**, and needs **UX and domain work**
a.foot: Behaviour **outside the variation points** still needs a **code change**, so choose the variation points from the **expected changes**.

q: An online learning platform has a layered monolith, five teams and frequent collisions between releases. It plans to add analytics, recommendations and partner integrations over two years. Compare a modular monolith, microservices and an event-driven approach for modifiability, and recommend one.

a.lead: **Recommend modularising first**, then extracting services where **team collisions** are worst, and publishing events for the new consumers.

sub: **Business modules contain changes** and avoid **distributed costs**
But everything still **deploys as one unit** → **release collisions remain**
**Independent deployment** per capability, if each **owns its data** and APIs **evolve compatibly**
But they add **operational cost**, and **shared tables** or **call chains** can still spread change
Analytics and recommendations can **subscribe to existing events** (CourseCompleted, LessonViewed) without **producer changes**
Only if the **payloads carry what they need**, with a **schema registry** and **compatibility rules**

q: A public REST API has about 200 external consumers you do not control. Over the next year you must add fields, rename one concept and change one response structure. Which code-level tactics keep the API evolvable?

items: **Request and response objects** with **optional fields** → additions don't break signatures
**Renamed concept**: add it alongside the old one, and **deprecate** the old name with a **support period**
**Structural change**: put it in a **new API version**, keeping the old one running during migration
**Encapsulate the implementation** behind the API, define the **shared data types once**, and use **standard formats**
**Test existing consumer contracts**
a.foot: Flexible **JSON syntax** alone does not guarantee **compatibility**.

q: During an incident, a payment fails somewhere across six microservices. It takes four hours to find the cause because logs are local to each container and have no common identifier. Redesign for analyzability.

items: **Automated error detection and alerting** → the failure is noticed rather than reported by users
**Centralise logs** with an agent, storage and searchable dashboard (for example **EFK**) → they survive container restarts
**Propagate a correlation id** from the entry point through every call and event → one request's entries can be retrieved together
**Log enough context**, such as inputs, the dependency called and the error
**Expose metrics** through **standard monitoring**
a.foot: The fix itself is then deployed like any other change, through the **reliable-change pipeline**.

q: A layered system's dependency rules are eroding, releases often break production, and rollbacks are manual. Design a pipeline that makes change reliable and stops further erosion.

items: **Keep everything in version control**, including **environment configuration as code**, with secrets in a **secrets manager**
**Automated tests** on each change: unit, integration and end-to-end

sub: A **dependency test** that fails on **layer violations**
Plus **performance, security, resiliency and observability** checks

items: **Automate deployment** with a **tested rollback path** and **reversible migrations**
**Hypothesis-driven testing** for risky changes
a.foot: Fitness functions **guard only what they encode**, so add rules as the architecture evolves.

q: A city's parking-permit system receives about 30,000 applications in the first week of each year and about 200 a week afterwards. It must take a nightly file from the vehicle registry, and two developers will maintain it. Stakeholders propose microservices. Do you agree? Which qualities and styles should drive the choice?

items: **Team and product**: **two developers** and **one product** → the **operational cost** (**discovery, gateways, automation**) outweighs **independent deployment**
**Driving qualities**: **elasticity** for the **January spike**, **cost** the rest of the year, and **reliable file-level integration** with the registry
**Style**: a **modular tiered application** on an **elastic platform**, with **file-level data flow** for the registry feed → meets them **more simply**
**Record** the qualities as **measurable scenarios** in a **utility tree** → the choice can be **revisited** if **more teams or functions** arrive

q: A ticket-resale marketplace runs in two regions. Buyers browse listings, sellers update prices, and a purchase must never sell the same ticket twice. Which operations favour availability during a partition, which messaging style suits notifying sellers, and which views would you give operations and auditors?

items: **Favour availability**: **browsing listings** and **showing prices**, with **short staleness**

sub: **Wait or reject during a partition**, because **selling a ticket twice** is unacceptable
An **ACID label does not settle partition behaviour**

items: **Notify sellers**: **publish/subscribe** → **email, push and analytics** subscribe **independently**

sub: **Operations**: **physical and deployment views** (**regions, nodes, failover**)
**Auditors**: **information-structure and deployment views** showing **where payment data lives** and **who can reach it**

q: A physical diagram already names products and server sizes, but the team has not agreed the business rules or the peak load. How would you get the architecture process back on track?

sub: **Stakeholders** (including **technical** ones), a **glossary**, a **system context**
Then **functional requirements** and **NFRs** with **measurable targets and conditions**

items: **Prioritise** the **architecturally significant** ones
**Derive the logical architecture** (**boundary, control and entity components**, **logical nodes**) and **verify** it

sub: **Size the nodes against the NFRs**
Keep the **existing product choices** as **recorded decisions** with **alternatives and assumptions** → they can be **overturned** if the requirements contradict them

q: IROne-style requirements: search 99.9% available within 3 s, other functions 99% within 5 s, 1000 concurrent users, and integration with hotel systems reachable only through messaging. A benchmark shows one application node handles 300 users at target. Outline the logical-to-physical decisions you would record.

sub: **Survive one failure**: **5** (**4 survivors x 300 = 1,200**)

items: **Other functions** can **share fewer nodes** if they are **isolated from search**
**Hotel boundaries → messaging**; flag the **transformation** in the **endpoint table** as **adapter work** to **specify and test**
**Record each choice** in the **Issue, Decision, Assumptions, Alternatives, Justification** format, especially the **300-user figure**
**Validate** it with a **proof of concept** under the **real request mix**

q: A system uses TLS, but an administrator account exports confidential records with no business need. Trace the risk and propose two different kinds of control.

sub: **Asset**: the **confidential records**
**Threat**: **misuse of privileged access**
**Vulnerability**: **excessive permissions** and **no monitoring**
**Assess likelihood and impact**, then **treat**

items: **Least privilege** and **role-based access** (**technical, preventive**)
**Audit logging** with **alerts on bulk exports** (**technical, detective**)
Backed by **regular access reviews** (**administrative, detective**)
a.foot: **TLS protects data in transit**; it does **not decide who should read the records**.

q: A telehealth service runs video consultations and stores consultation notes. TLS terminates at a load balancer in the DMZ, clinicians log in with a password, and a vendor supports the video servers remotely. Identify the top three risks and choose a control for each, stating its type and category.

sub: Control: **MFA** (**technical, preventive**)

items.t: **Plaintext at the DMZ load balancer** → exposes notes if it is **compromised** (**information disclosure**)
sub: Control: **encrypt the notes for the back end**, or **terminate TLS deeper**, and **harden the load balancer** (**technical, preventive**)
Control: an **MFA-protected, logged jump host** on a **segregated admin network** (**technical, preventive and detective**)

a.foot: Add **IDS** and **log review** so the design is **not only preventive**, and **record the residual risk**.

q: Two app servers replace one, but the database and network remain shared. Peak-time latency still fails its target. What should you inspect before adding a third?

items: **Find the real bottleneck**: measure **response time, queueing, throughput** and **per-resource utilisation**
**Shared database saturated?** → a third app server **adds load to it** without **adding throughput**
**Map required dependencies** and **shared failure points**: two app servers do nothing for a **database or network failure**
**Decision**: add app servers only if **that tier is the limit**; otherwise **scale or offload the database** (**caching**, **read replicas**, **fewer visits per request**)

q: Two app servers in parallel, 99% available each, run at 70% CPU during peak. A teammate claims the tier is now 99.99% available. Do you agree?

items: **Assumption**: the **99.99%** figure assumes **either server can carry the full load alone**
**At 70% CPU**: if one fails, the survivor would need **140%** of its capacity → it **saturates**, **queues grow without bound**, service **effectively down**

sub: Size so **one server can carry the peak** (each **below about 50%** at peak, **preferably lower** to keep **response times** acceptable)
Or **add a third server**

a.foot: Then the **parallel calculation is justified**, provided **failover works** and **failures are independent**.

q: Search works from cache during a database outage, but checkout fails. Is the system available?

a.lead: **Judge each function against its own requirement**: **cached search is available**, **checkout is not**.
items: **Agreed service**: if it counts **checkout as critical**, the service is **unavailable for that purpose**, whatever the **search page** shows
**Circuit breaker and cache** → **graceful degradation**
**Checkout availability** needs a **redundant data tier** or a **degraded mode**, such as **holding orders for later confirmation**, if the **business accepts** it

q: The disk may fill in eight weeks, procurement takes seven, and moving to a new store also risks breaking clients. How would you combine capacity planning and maintainability?

sub: Compare **linear and exponential fits**
Include **logs and indexes**
The **earlier date** may already be **inside the lead time**

items: **Capacity**: start **procurement or interim capacity now**, with a **buffer**

sub: Put **storage behind a stable interface**
Use **compatibility checks**
**Stage the migration** with a **rollback path**

items: **After the change**: **monitoring** and **fitness checks** to confirm **capacity** and catch **failures**

q: Forecast peak demand is 80 requests/s, and each node sustainably handles 35 requests/s. How many nodes do you need to survive the loss of one node, and what would make that number wrong?

a.lead: **Four nodes**: **three survivors give 105 requests/s**, while **two would give only 70**.

sub: The **35 requests/s** came from a **benchmark with a different request mix**
**Sub-linear scaling** (**shared data** or **crosstalk**, per **Amdahl and USL**)
A **shared dependency** such as the **database saturates first**

items: **Verify** with a **load test at the production mix**, and **test failover**

q: A SaaS product's pricing rules change monthly, and its tenant count doubles every year. A teammate proposes per-tenant code branches to handle client-specific rules. Respond, covering both maintainability and capacity.

items: **Maintainability**: every **fix must be repeated across branches** → the **cost of change grows with every tenant**
**Deferred binding** instead: **per-tenant configuration or workflows** loaded **at run time** behind **defined variation points**

items.t: **Capacity**: the **doubling tenant count** drives both **cumulative storage** and **peak server load**
sub: **Forecast both from tenant growth**, using **application metrics** such as **tenants** and **requests per tenant**

items: **Load tests** to check the scaling, since a **configuration lookup on every request** adds work

q: A resort reservation system must take 1,500 concurrent bookings at the 8 am release of holiday slots, survive the loss of any one server, and let the business change its booking rules every quarter without a release. How would you turn these goals into a defensible architecture, and what evidence would you need before committing?

items: **Measurable scenarios**: write each goal as one, e.g. **'90% of bookings confirmed within 3 s with 1,500 concurrent users at 8 am'**; rank them in a **utility tree**
**Logical design**: derive **boundary, control and entity components**
**Survive one server loss**: map the **booking control one to many** across nodes sized so the **survivors still carry the peak**
**Quarterly rule changes**: put the rules behind a **configuration or rules-engine variation point**; **record that decision** with its **assumptions**

sub: **Benchmark** the booking scenario with the **real request mix**
**Calculate end-to-end availability** including **shared dependencies**
**Test failover**

a.foot: **Benchmarks rarely scale linearly**, and a **topology label proves nothing**.

q: Two million smart meters each send a reading every 15 minutes, and most send in the first minute of each window. The current design writes every reading synchronously into one primary database with one read replica, and it is falling behind. Propose a plan to scale the writes and name two side effects to monitor.

sub: **Average ≈ 2,200 writes/s**
**Real peak ≈ 33,000/s** if most of the **2 million** arrive within **60 s**

items: **Durable queue or event stream** in front of the database → ingestion **absorbs the burst**; writers **drain it at a sustainable rate**
**Partition (shard)** the readings **by meter id** across **several primaries** (a **read replica adds no write capacity**), and **batch the inserts**

sub: **Queue lag**: how **stale the latest reading** is, against any **freshness requirement**
**Uneven shards** or **hot partitions**

a.foot: **Cross-shard queries and reports** become harder → feed them from the **stream** or a separate **analytics store**.

q: A teammate proposes 'number of monthly active users' as the metric showing that a booking platform is scalable and highly available. Do you agree? What would you measure instead?

a.lead: **No.** **Monthly active users** measures **adoption volume**, not how the system behaves **as load grows** or how often it is **unavailable**.
items: **Why not**: a high count says nothing about **response time at peak**, and could **rise while users suffer outages**
**Scalability**: **throughput and response-time percentiles against load** (e.g. **p90 response at 1x, 2x and 4x peak**), and how **throughput grows as nodes are added**
**Availability**: **(agreed service time - downtime) / agreed service time** per **critical function**, plus **MTTR**

q: A logical packaging and deployment model puts the web front end, booking service and payment adapter in one deployable on a single node in the DMZ, with the database on the same node. Identify the undesirable decisions and propose corrective actions.

sub: Compromising the **web front end** exposes the **booking logic, payment adapter and data**
**Fix**: keep only the **web tier or reverse proxy** in the DMZ; place the **services and database** behind an **inner firewall** with only the **required traffic** allowed

items.t: **One node, one deployable** → **single point of failure** that **cannot scale by tier**
sub: **Fix**: **separate the deployables**, run the **booking service one to many** behind a **load balancer**, give the **database its own redundant nodes**

items.t: **Payment adapter bundled with unrelated code** → a payment change forces a **full redeploy**
sub: **Fix**: make it **its own unit** behind a **stable interface**

a.foot: Each correction adds **nodes and operating cost**, which must be **justified** against the **availability, security and modifiability scenarios**.
